title: Local complex Hessian forms and holomorphic pullback
statement:
Use the real and complex fields [def-weil-field]. Let $d,e\geq0$, let $U\subseteq\mathbf C^d$ and $V\subseteq\mathbf C^e$ be open, and let $\phi:U\to\mathbf R$ be $C^\infty$ in real coordinates. Write $z_j=x_j+iy_j$, $\partial_{z_j}=\tfrac12(\partial_{x_j}-i\partial_{y_j})$ and $\partial_{\bar z_j}=\tfrac12(\partial_{x_j}+i\partial_{y_j})$. On differential forms, $\partial$ and $\bar\partial$ mean differentiation of the coefficients followed by exterior multiplication by $dz_j$ and $d\bar z_j$, respectively. Define
$$D_U\phi=\frac{i}{2\pi}\partial\bar\partial\phi=\frac{i}{2\pi}\sum_{r,s=1}^d\frac{\partial^2\phi}{\partial z_r\partial\bar z_s}\,dz_r\wedge d\bar z_s.$$
Here differential forms are alternating multilinear functions on real tangent vectors with complex coefficients; real means fixed by conjugation, closed means exterior derivative zero, and type $(1,1)$ means a sum of $dz_r\wedge d\bar z_s$ terms. Then $D_U\phi$ is a smooth real closed form of type $(1,1)$, and $D_U$ is real-linear. If $F:V\to U$ is holomorphic (its coordinate functions are locally convergent complex power series), then $F^*(D_U\phi)=D_V(\phi\circ F)$, where pullback evaluates a form on the real differential of $F$. If $h:U\to\mathbf C$ is holomorphic and nowhere zero, then $\log|h|^2$ is smooth and $D_U(\log|h|^2)=0$.

source.place: WANTED locally. Read online https://www-fourier.univ-grenoble-alpes.fr/~demailly/manuscripts/agbook.pdf: I §3.C, (3.13)–(3.19), printed pp.23–25 (Wirtinger calculus and pullback); V §13, line-bundle curvature change of frame, and VI §4 Example (4.4), printed p.297. Log-modulus consequence follows by differentiating h and its conjugate; no global logarithm is assumed.

proof.text: Work locally on the open real coordinate domain. By [lem-sfb-real-smooth-differentiation], every real partial derivative of $\phi$ is smooth, and real differentiation is linear and obeys the product rule. Evaluation of a real differential on a fixed coordinate vector is a continuous real-linear map, so iterating this observation also gives smoothness of all coefficient derivatives. By [lem-sfb-real-second-derivative-symmetry], any two real coordinate derivatives commute on a smooth coefficient. Expanding $\partial_{z_r}$ and $\partial_{\bar z_s}$ as the specified constant linear combinations therefore shows that any two Wirtinger derivatives commute on smooth coefficients. Real differentiation commutes with conjugation by the real chain rule, since conjugation is real-linear; hence $\overline{\partial_{z_r}a}=\partial_{\bar z_r}\overline a$ and $\overline{\partial_{\bar z_r}a}=\partial_{z_r}\overline a$.

proof.text: Put $H_{rs}=\partial_{z_r}\partial_{\bar z_s}\phi$. Step 1 gives $\overline{H_{rs}}=\partial_{\bar z_r}\partial_{z_s}\phi=H_{sr}$ because $\phi$ is real. Conjugating the displayed formula for $D_U\phi$ gives $(-i/2\pi)\sum_{r,s}H_{sr}\,d\bar z_r\wedge dz_s$. Reversing the wedge factors and renaming $r,s$ recovers $D_U\phi$, proving reality. Smoothness follows from the smooth coefficients, and type $(1,1)$ is exactly its displayed expansion. For real constants $a,b$, coefficient differentiation gives $H(a\phi+b\psi)=aH(\phi)+bH(\psi)$ by [lem-sfb-real-smooth-differentiation]; multiplication by $i/2\pi$ proves real-linearity.

source.place: Demailly, Complex Analytic and Differential Geometry, I §3.C, equations (3.13)–(3.19), printed pp.23–25; read online from the author URL in the item source. Coordinate calculation expanded here from the cited Mathlib calculus statements.

proof.text:
The real-coordinate formula for exterior differentiation, rewritten using $dz_k=dx_k+i\,dy_k$ and $d\bar z_k=dx_k-i\,dy_k$, gives
$$d(D_U\phi)=\frac{i}{2\pi}\sum_{k,r,s}\left((\partial_{z_k}H_{rs})dz_k\wedge dz_r\wedge d\bar z_s+(\partial_{\bar z_k}H_{rs})d\bar z_k\wedge dz_r\wedge d\bar z_s\right).$$
In the first sum $\partial_{z_k}H_{rs}=\partial_{z_r}H_{ks}$ by step 1: apply second-derivative symmetry to the smooth coefficient $\partial_{\bar z_s}\phi$. Terms indexed by $(k,r)$ cancel by alternatingness; diagonal terms vanish. In the second sum $\partial_{\bar z_k}H_{rs}=\partial_{\bar z_s}H_{rk}$, by commuting the derivatives on smooth coefficients. Interchanging $k,s$ negates the three-fold wedge, so these terms cancel too. The smoothness and commutations used here are precisely [lem-sfb-real-smooth-differentiation] and [lem-sfb-real-second-derivative-symmetry]. Thus the form is closed.

source.place: Demailly, Complex Analytic and Differential Geometry, I §3.C, equations (3.13)–(3.19), printed pp.23–25; read online from the author URL in the item source. Coordinate calculation expanded here from the cited Mathlib calculus statements.

proof.text: For any holomorphic coordinate function $g$ on an open subset of $\mathbf C^e$, [lem-sfb-analytic-real-smooth] gives real smoothness and a complex-linear real differential. Write $g_{x_a}=Dg[e_a]$. Complex-linearity gives $g_{y_a}=Dg[i e_a]=i g_{x_a}$, whence $\partial_{\bar w_a}g=0$ and $\partial_{w_a}g=g_{x_a}$. By [lem-sfb-complex-analytic-derivative-rules], the complex differential of $g$ is analytic; evaluation at the fixed complex coordinate vector is complex-linear and analytic by [lem-sfb-complex-analytic-function-operations], so each $g_{w_a}$ is holomorphic as well. The same statements apply componentwise to $F$; the finite-tuple clause of [lem-sfb-complex-analytic-function-operations] makes $F$ analytic and thus real smooth. Conjugation and step 1 also give $\partial_{w_a}\overline g=0$ and $\partial_{\bar w_a}\overline g=\overline{g_{w_a}}$.

source.place: Demailly, Complex Analytic and Differential Geometry, I §3.C, equations (3.13)–(3.19), printed pp.23–25; read online from the author URL in the item source. Coordinate calculation expanded here from the cited Mathlib calculus statements.

proof.text:
Set $F_{r,a}=\partial_{w_a}F_r$. The real chain rule in [lem-sfb-real-smooth-differentiation], expressed in the Wirtinger basis and using step 4, gives
$$\partial_{\bar w_b}(\phi\circ F)=\sum_s(\partial_{\bar z_s}\phi)(F)\,\overline{F_{s,b}}.$$
Differentiate in $w_a$. Step 4 applied to the holomorphic $F_{s,b}$ shows $\partial_{w_a}\overline{F_{s,b}}=0$, and the remaining chain-rule terms give
$$\partial_{w_a}\partial_{\bar w_b}(\phi\circ F)=\sum_{r,s}H_{rs}(F)F_{r,a}\overline{F_{s,b}}.$$
On the other hand pullback, by its definition on tangent vectors, sends $dz_r$ to $\sum_a F_{r,a}dw_a$ and $d\bar z_s$ to $\sum_b\overline{F_{s,b}}d\bar w_b$. Substitution in the formula for $D_U\phi$ yields exactly the preceding coefficients multiplied by $i/2\pi$. Hence $F^*D_U\phi=D_V(\phi\circ F)$; the composite is smooth by the same real smooth composition rule.

source.place: Demailly, Complex Analytic and Differential Geometry, I §3.C, equations (3.13)–(3.19), printed pp.23–25; read online from the author URL in the item source. Coordinate calculation expanded here from the cited Mathlib calculus statements.

proof.text:
Let $h$ be as in the final clause and put $q=|h|^2=(\operatorname{Re}h)^2+(\operatorname{Im}h)^2$. By [lem-sfb-analytic-real-smooth], $h$ is real smooth. Real and imaginary parts are real-linear, so [lem-sfb-real-smooth-differentiation] gives smoothness of $q$; since $h$ never vanishes, $q>0$, and its logarithm is smooth by the real logarithm and composition clauses. The real differential of the polynomial $|\zeta|^2$ at $\zeta$ on $v$ is $v\overline\zeta+\zeta\overline v$, by the product rule and real-linearity of conjugation. Thus the real chain rule and step 4 give
$$\partial_{z_r}\log q=q^{-1}(\partial_{z_r}h)\overline h=\frac{\partial_{z_r}h}{h}.$$
The division is valid pointwise since $h\ne0$, and $q=h\overline h$. No branch of the complex logarithm has been introduced.

source.place: Demailly, Complex Analytic and Differential Geometry, I §3.C, equations (3.13)–(3.19), printed pp.23–25; read online from the author URL in the item source. Coordinate calculation expanded here from the cited Mathlib calculus statements.

proof.text:
By [lem-sfb-complex-analytic-derivative-rules] and [lem-sfb-complex-analytic-function-operations], each $h_{z_r}$ and $1/h$ is holomorphic, so $h_{z_r}/h$ is holomorphic. Step 4 then makes its $\bar z_s$ derivative zero. Applying [lem-sfb-real-second-derivative-symmetry] to the smooth real function $\log q$ from step 6, and expanding the Wirtinger derivatives as in step 1, gives
$$\partial_{z_r}\partial_{\bar z_s}\log q=\partial_{\bar z_s}\partial_{z_r}\log q=\partial_{\bar z_s}(h_{z_r}/h)=0.$$
Every coefficient in $D_U(\log|h|^2)$ therefore vanishes. Empty domains require no pointwise checks; when $d=0$ or $e=0$ the relevant sums and differential-form components are empty, so all formulas remain valid.
